Only about, I would say, 20 to 25 percent of the nation has PFOA challenges in the way that the old cities of the Northeast and old cities in the Midwest have. A lot of it is because we have PFOS, PFOS was used in fertilizers and in pesticides for a long time, much of that has been discontinued, however PFOS is still continued to be used in plastics in many of the fire reduction clothing and the chemicals that are used for other purposes. And the regulations are not imposing themselves on the source of PFAS. They're imposing themselves on the water system. 20% of the PFAS you are exposed to comes through the water systems. The rest of it does come through plastics, through the air, through soil, through other means of production, and you may actually have more access to PFAS if you drink your water through plastic water bottles all the time than using the water out of your tap. However, the regulations are very strong. The state of Pennsylvania up until now has had really good regulations, 14 parts per trillion has been one of the most aggressive of the standards of the states in the country and we have been able to stay within that limit except for periods of severe drought as we had over this last year. If the standard goes to four parts per trillion, then it really becomes an all bets are off situation where one has to look at extraordinarily expensive options and we would need to very strongly seek other kinds of funding and support we would need federal support we need all kinds of other ways of being able to take that on and what you'll see as we've talked about it in terms of the long-term control plan is we're also trying to space out the requested funding for the long-term for the consent decree initiatives so that it minimizes or does not overturn the apple cart in terms of how much it's going to cost over time to take care of these infrastructure matters. So the big items that are unpredictable are the lead service lines and the PFAS, PFOA. Other than that, we are generally in very good shape in terms of being able to manage infrastructure in a way that that can allow us to be much more predictable about the costs involved
